HBO Bet Big and Won With Succession

The cast of the knives-out drama tell us how they made the summer’s sharpest show.
By Sam SchubePhotography by Erik Tanner
November 27, 2018

The success of Succession, HBO’s baroque satire of an ailing media titan and his variously brilliant, buffoonish, and meth-smoking family members, might be chalked up to its calculated flattery of the 99 percent. Yes, the show suggests, the richest of us have it good: They own gigantic homes, masturbate onto their office windows, and carry obscenely large golf umbrellas through Manhattan. But all of that, Succession carefully illustrates, comes at the cost of health, family, and anything approaching genuine human intimacy. A sumptuous Sunday-night HBO drama with a serious production budget turned out to have a not-so-quiet subversive streak and ventured an idea rare on cable TV: Being rich might really fucking suck.

The creative team includes executive producer Adam McKay and creator Jesse Armstrong, who have earned their places at the barricades: McKay with his decreasingly fantastical looks at the horror of American wealth (Talladega Nights, The Big Short), and Armstrong with razor-sharp British comedies (Peep Show, The Thick of It). And while Logan Roy, the volcanic patriarch played by Brian Cox, sat at the center, Succession’s true revelation was the youngish cast assembled around him. Most notably, the Roy children: Kendall (Jeremy Strong), the in-recovery would-be CEO who plots a coup against Dad; Roman (Kieran Culkin), the wisecracking shitheel who undermines Kendall’s coup; and Siobhan, or Shiv (Sarah Snook), the political consultant backing an enemy politician. Two more characters just outside the family, but trying feverishly to work their way in, have risen to the fore: Shiv’s husband, genial psychopath Tom Wambsgans (Matthew Macfadyen); and gawky, permanently ill-at-ease, occasionally Machiavellian cousin Greg Hirsch (Nicholas Braun).

All five spent the summer crafting takeover bids, gobbling songbirds, and most resonantly, lobbing insults. All of a sudden, a show that had started slowly became perhaps the show of the season—and indisputably the show of its time. Here’s how it happened.

Quite Greek

The pilot introduces us to the Roy family, controllers of America’s fifth-largest media (and amusement-park) conglomerate. When an aging Logan suffers a stroke, his children jockey for position. Armstrong had written a screenplay about the Murdoch family which provided the initial spark for the show. (All involved insist that the family is definitely not Rupert Murdoch’s, which tracks: You can spot traces of all your favorite oligarchs, not just the Murdochs, in these monsters.)

Jeremy Strong (Kendall Roy): I’d worked with Adam [McKay] on The Big Short. I went to lunch at his house, and he said that he had this script that was kind of loosely about the Murdochs—sort of a King Lear–meets-the-media-industrial-complex kind of thing. It sounded really compelling to me, and I read the script and fell in love with it. Adam brought me in, and then I had to go fight for the role. When you finally come to a piece of work that you feel like you could really serve, and it would give you a chance as an actor to be fully expressed and fire on all cylinders, the stakes feel so high.

Matthew Macfadyen (Tom Wambsgans): It was dark and acerbic. I didn’t know how to categorize it. I think it’s quite exciting when you don’t really know what it is. I thought at times, “It’s quite Greek.” It’s the great big perennial themes, and also it’s funny as fuck. And it’s ridiculous, and it’s heightened. But then, it’s not that heightened.

Strong: I tend to get highfalutin, but I read that [Carl] Jung said, “Only that which is really ourselves has the power to heal.” And it’s not often that you find a role where you think, “Oh, I can bring a lot of my own turmoil and my own struggle and pain and yearning and ambition.” Which is all a very volcanic thing, which this gave a real outlet to. A kind of channel. A lifetime’s worth of yearning to make a mark into.

“Why is it I identify with this guy so fucking much? I still don’t know why, and I don’t want to know.”

Sarah Snook (Siobhan “Shiv” Roy): The speed of the [pilot] script sort of sucks you in by accident. I got to the end, and I was like, “Huh! Well, even if I don’t get to do it, I’m gonna watch it ’cause I wanna know what happens.” By the end, you didn’t realize how invested you already were.

Kieran Culkin (Roman Roy): They sent it to me to read for Greg, and right away I felt I was completely wrong for it. But I liked it enough to keep reading it. And then it was pretty much right away when I read Roman. He walks in, says, “Hey, hey, motherfuckers!”—well, who’s he? By the bottom of that page, I was like, “Oh, I kind of get this guy’s language.” Not to be kissing the writers’ asses, but they do a great fucking job with their dialogue, and I just felt immediately comfortable.

Snook: I felt like, “Ah, there’s no way I’m gonna get this, so I’m not stressed.” I really just was like, “Eh, this is out of my league. I’ll just come and do it and get out of here. Free trip to L.A. for a weekend and see my friends. This’ll be great.”

Culkin: I was going to ask, “Can I read for Roman?” But instead I just decided to put myself on tape. This has maybe happened twice ever, this being one of the two times where I had so much fun in the audition that I walked away going, “I don’t even care if I get it,” because I just had the best day working on that.

Nicholas Braun (Greg Hirsch): Adam McKay is a guy that I’ve worshipped since I started watching his movies—you know, Anchorman and stuff. When I heard it was him, I was just like, “This is fuckin’ huge!” It’s HBO, so it was like, “This is gonna be awesome regardless.” It’s a dream come true to be on a Sunday-night show.

A Very Stark Depiction of What Money Is

The super-rich are not like the rest of us—a lesson each cast member learned in their own way.

Snook: The show is a credit to [casting director] Francine Maisler putting the right people together at the right time in their lives. It felt unnaturally easy—to be, like, “Oh yeah, Kieran is that kind of person with Roman. Let’s just turn that part of Kieran’s personality up 5,000 percent and he becomes Roman; great, we’ll just use that.” There’s an element of all of us, I guess, in the characters.

Culkin: Why is it I identify with this guy so fucking much? I still don’t know why, and I don’t want to know.

Braun: I read Greg, and I was like, “This is a guy that makes sense to me,” even though he makes no sense at all as a guy. He’s super bold, but also completely oblivious to what he even is doing anywhere. That combination made sense. The dialogue was perfectly choppy, and I could stumble through stuff in a way that made sense. Jesse wrote dashes and ellipses and things. The way that words came out made sense. He built that hesitation and the fucking gulping, and the whole thing. Kind of like how I’m talking right now.

Culkin: Whenever I try to do any kind of external research, it ends up fucking with me. I thought maybe for this character I should look into the lifestyle of the way these guys are, and it started fucking with me. But it seemed to me that Roman also doesn’t quite understand what this world is. He wants to be COO, and he wants to fight hard for it, but I don’t think he actually understands what being a COO means.

Strong: I wanted to really drill down in the world of the media landscape. There was a lot of great stuff to read about the Murdochs—there was that great James B. Stewart book DisneyWar. [The book relates the stupendous rise, hilarious dickishness, and precipitous fall of Michael Eisner’s tenure at the Walt Disney Company.—Ed.] It really is like the War of the Roses. It’s not simply this Machiavellian greed and ambition. It’s much deeper than that. As an actor, you’re looking for the why, you’re looking for what is propelling this person and why do they need these things. That book was a real gold mine in terms of understanding the drive.

Braun: Jeremy suggested I read DisneyWar. He said, “You’ll understand the amusement-park world and stuff. It will be really good for you.” I started reading it, and I was like, “This isn’t really helping me, because I’m supposed to know nothing.”

Macfadyen: I just waited until the first script came in and then gobbled it up and then started. Unless you need to learn to do something specifically, like fly a helicopter or learn the saxophone, the writing’s so good that it’s all there. [Tom is] half suave, half dickhead.

Braun: I did do a little research. I asked HBO if they would set up a tour around Time Warner. We went to the CNN newsroom floor, and the tour guide was like, “Hey, do you want to meet [CNN president] Jeff Zucker’s assistant?” She was super nice, and I asked her some questions about what it’s like to be an assistant. And then I saw Jeff in the office. And really before anybody knew it, I jetted into Jeff’s office. I was like, “Hey, Jeff, how are you doing? My name is Nick, I’m playing blah-blah on a new show, and I’m super excited to meet you. Anything you can tell me about executive assistance?” He didn’t look up once. He stayed looking right at his computer screen, and he said, “She can help you out there.” I was like, “All right, well, love everything that you do.” And he shook my hand without looking at me from the computer screen. Like, limp—he didn’t even care. I doubt he even registered that moment.

Snook: I listened to a lot of American politics, a lot of business podcasts, like Planet Money. I bought this book called Generation Wealth, by Lauren Greenfield. I was like, “Let me just see what money is in America.” And that actually was amazing, ’cause that was a very stark depiction of what money is. Just getting a sense of the entitlement that someone may experience if they’ve grown up with money all the time. Someone who doesn’t have a safety net operates in the world very differently from someone who does have a safety net. And then someone who does have a safety net, but is not aware of it, operates differently again.

Strong: I thought that Kendall was into Bruce Lee, and I had bought all these Bruce Lee books that I was reading as sort of daily calendars. I was thinking, “What can I learn to do in kung fu in, like, four days?” There was something called the Ma Bu Punch, which you can get some great YouTube videos on, so I just practiced the shit out of that. I would have loved to have, like, three months to really perfect that.

Braun: I also just wanted to be uncomfortable next to people. So before we started shooting, I would just be in public places and talk to people. In the airport, on my way to shoot the pilot, I just found myself in kiosks and the massage parlor, talking to people for too long and getting used to that energy. At first I was like, “Oh, this is the point where this will get uncomfortable.” And people were still tolerating it. So you just really had to hang in there. I was in, like, the earphone place in the airport, and I just had to keep asking about earphones to see: When is the time when they walk away?

Macfadyen: We had a [wardrobe] fitting, and I suddenly put the turtleneck on, and it was like, “Of course.” ’Cause he would have picked it out very carefully for the family Thanksgiving. And we just thought, “Yeah.” I looked sort of like a demented mime artist who thinks he’s James Bond.

Anything Goes

Early on, executive producer Adam McKay instituted his preferred improv-heavy process. Adaptation proved necessary even before the pilot was shot, and it presented a challenge for the crew. Wild scenarios in later episodes—Kendall’s relapse in New Mexico, a wedding in Britain—added to the fun.

Macfadyen: We did a read-through of the pilot on the eve of Election Night. So we all went to this gathering at Adam McKay’s house after the read-through to kind of watch the returns.

Snook: [McKay] found out [about the election results] at about nine o’clock. He was like, “Yep. It’s done.” And we’re like, “No…no. You’re overreacting. It’s not happening yet.” And then there’s a silence. He’s like, “Well, at least we’re making the right show.”

Macfadyen: The party was, like…[makes sputtering noise]. But you think, “Anything that you put in the show, it’s kind of: Well, that’s fine now, because anything goes.”

Snook: I have a very vivid memory of Jeremy at the end of the night, saying goodbye. I remember saying, I think, “You good? Are you all right? You gonna catch a cab?” And he’s like, “No, I’m just gonna walk for a bit,” and he just walked off into the night. So if that’s not the image for what’s going on, right now…

Strong: One of the reasons I loved working with McKay the most is because he comes from that [improv] background. It just opens up the environment in a way where you have permission to wander off the path a little bit and go off-roading and fuck around.

Braun: I really like it. Especially with Greg, because the more stuff that Greg says that’s out of line, the better it works.

Snook: I had to get over my self-doubt. I’m doing new lines or improvised dialogue in an American accent, so it’s getting rid of the fear. Once we did that, it seemed to flow smoother. [I’d improvised in] an Australian accent, but not in an American accent being a billionaire’s daughter.

Culkin: Adam’s way of working actually terrified me at the beginning. I’ve not done that shit. I get really insecure if they don’t write the exact line. So he would say, “Yeah, we’re going to do a couple of takes scripted, and then we’re just going to leave it up to you. Or I might in the middle of a take throw out a joke at you, and you’re going to have to deliver it.” And I’m like, “This is your thing, not mine.”

Braun: I was like, “Am I ruining scenes by being as weird as I am? Or just lurking and having this other energy?” But I guess that’s what Greg is in this world—the guy who doesn’t say the right thing almost ever.

Strong: We sort of went down a K-hole in New Mexico. I feel like I did. They wouldn’t let us smoke meth, so I don’t know what we were smoking, but it felt like we were in this gauzy, fucked-up fever-dream place.

Culkin: By the time we were doing [episodes] seven, eight, nine, I was like, “It feels kind of like we have a show here.”

Snook: When we were getting scenes that were with the siblings all together, working that dynamic, I was like, “Okay, this is the show. This is where it’s most interesting.” And I think what Jesse and the rest of the writers did, which was genius, is putting them all together into a room, in these circumstances where family should triumph. And yet this is the very moment where they tear each other to shreds. They eviscerate each other.

Less Wonderment

The ass end of that evisceration was typically Braun’s Cousin Greg. A fan of marijuana and California Pizza Kitchen (“They make a Cajun chicken linguine just the way I like it”), Greg became an audience favorite, thanks in large part to his jousting with Macfadyen’s Tom. Even months after production wrapped, the dynamic remains. I’m scheduled to speak with Braun after my interview with Strong, which is running long. When I tell Strong that I need to go, and why, he lights up: “I mean, fucking Cousin Greg? He can wait.”

Macfadyen: He’s the tallest man in the world. He’s like six feet six.

Culkin: I have a hard time keeping it together with Nick. And that goes for just, like, everyone across the board who meets him. When we first worked together, I invited him over to a birthday thing that I had, and everybody that came over was like, “Who the hell is this guy? This guy is great!” Both men and women flock to him in such a flirty way without quite understanding why they want to flirt with him, you know? And to have a photographer not keep it to himself but actually come out and say “less wonderment” [moments earlier, at the photo shoot, the photographer had requested “less wonderment” from Braun], that could only happen with Nick.

Macfadyen: I had terrible giggles. Really bad. We set each other off, almost every scene. I had to say “Did you bitch me out, pig-man?” right in his face. “Did you bitch me out?” That was really, really difficult. And the slightest twinkle…I’d see it, and I’d be gone.

Snook: It’s just delicious watching them. I wanted to be there on those days.

Braun: Every scene we had was difficult. I’d prepare at night, and I’d be like, “All right, I know what I’m doing. I’m not going to laugh tomorrow.” Because you feel so guilty when you’re breaking up. And without fail, we would laugh in all of our scenes. By the end of the season, we started to figure it out. We started to be able to break for a second and then tighten it up really quickly. [Macfadyen is] just a fucking amazing guy to work with and so generous. I would want to do our scenes for hours and hours. We were shooting on film, so it was always pretty quick. But if they let us, I would burn all that film with him.

Strong: I brought Nick out to the Hamptons a couple of weekends ago. It was great. We ended up at a party with the Clintons and Paul McCartney, and they were big fans of Cousin Greg.

Braun: [Jeremy] spent the summer in Copenhagen, and he was like, “I’m coming back to the East Coast. I’m going to my friend’s family’s house in Bridgehampton. They would love you to come.” They’d seen the show, so they were like, “Bring Cousin Greg.” I take a packed Long Island Rail Road train with my weekend bag. [Strong] picks me up in this great classic red convertible and he’s super well-dressed and just in the vibe. We put the top down immediately, ’cause otherwise my head was going to hit the ceiling. Friday morning we wake up, and I go to breakfast, and I’m sitting next to the woman of the household. She’s on her phone, and she’s frustrated, and I’m like, “What’s going on?” And she’s like, “Oh, just dealing with the Secret Service.” And I’m like, “I totally get it. I’ve been there a million times. Those guys are kooks.” And I didn’t ask any more questions, ’cause I wanted to play it cool. And then later on, Secret Service come and check the house.

Long story short, I’m told I’m gonna meet Hillary [Clinton]. I go and shake her hand, and I’m so excited and nervous; I think she’s amazing. And then I see Bill, and he’s got a crowd around him, totally enthralled, and he’s regaling them with some story. Kind of Greg-style, I just go over and sort of lurk. He finishes his story, and the first thing he does, he puts his hand out to me, and says, “How’re you doing? Bill.” I’m like, “Hey. Nick. Huge fan.” And somebody in the circle says, “Oh, this is Nick Braun. He’s on this show. You’ll love it, Bill: Succession.” And he immediately takes an interest. I think he’d heard of the show, and he starts talking about Rupert Murdoch, and other corporate families, and goes in on stories. Jeremy walks up, and he sees that I’m in a circle with Bill, and he’s just, “What is happening? How did you even…?”

Strong: People in power that I’ve encountered are compelled by the show.

Snook: [Braun] sent a photo. I was like, “What the fuck? What is this? Where is your mind?”

Braun: I was just sort of like, “At what point is Bill gonna want me to walk away, so he can talk to people he actually knows or cares about?” But we talked for a while. He really loved talking to me and Jeremy and hearing about the show. At one point he said, “I’m gonna go home and I’m gonna watch the show—tonight. I’m gonna go watch it right now.” And I was like, “That’s awesome. If you’d like to do a guest spot, we’d love to have you.” He said, “I just might do that. That’d be fun.” It was so Greg-y.

Will Anybody Care?

Succession hit the air in June but bubbled under the radar until the fourth episode—“Sad Sack Wasp Trap,” which found Cox’s patriarch recovering and the family members maneuvering into prime dickish position. From there, it was off to the races.*

Macfadyen: When we were shooting, we were like, “Will anybody care about these entitled fuckheads with more money than God? Their trials and tribulations, their jerking for power, who cares?” A part of me did think, “Well, maybe it’s the last thing people want.”

Culkin: I haven’t asked anybody, any of the producers on the show, and I probably shouldn’t be talking about it publicly, but I’ve just been doing it and no one’s told me to shut up. I’ve been saying that this show does take a while. But it’s a hard sell to tell somebody, “You’re going to have to invest five hours before you get to a show that’s actually pretty good.” [My wife] said by four it grabbed her. And I’ve been asking people, and it seems by either episode four or episode six.

Macfadyen: When [Logan] was taken away from the hospital and they move back into their apartment, we went back to work. The bullying of Greg began. That was different.

Braun: As the season grew, you understood, “Oh, I get to laugh at them.” Whereas in the beginning, I think, people weren’t sure exactly. Like, “Am I supposed to feel like I love all these people right away? Because I can’t.”

Macfadyen: People are fascinated by wealth and power, but it’s family, I think, that’s the key thing. You go, “Oh God, that’s my idiot brother with delusions of grandeur” or “that’s my frightening sister” or “that’s my slightingly unnerving stepmother.” You can identify with all of them, regardless of whether they’re billionaires.

Strong: I do think this has touched on the dark heart of our country in some sideways way. It’s obviously not about our president. But it’s not not about his family. In a way, it’s about this sort of poison that is at the heart of corporate culture, which is the nucleus of our culture right now. I think Adam and Jesse were very interested in tracing the genesis of that poison and that aggression. I think a lot of it is about this familial aggression getting unleashed on a global stage.

Braun: I think the biggest gauge was people on the street talking about it. The first few episodes, we didn’t have that. And then, all of a sudden, in a subway station in Columbus Circle in New York, this tourist family came up to me. They were like, “You’re gonna get all the money! Cousin Greg! Oh, my God, can we have a picture with Cousin Greg? You’re gonna get everything. We know it.” And I was like, “Damn, people are fucking stoked. This has penetrated into something. They believe in Greg!”
